Guerry Social Science Data in 1830's France.

Source: R/data.R
guerry_sf.Rd

Department-level social science data in France in the 1830's, collected by Andre-Michel Guerry. Each row corresponds to a particular department (region) in the country of France.

Usage

guerry_sf

Format

An sf object with an NTF (Paris) / Lambert zone II polygonal projection with 85 rows and 14 columns:

  • region: the region of the department, a factor with 5 levels (C for Central, E for East, N for North, S for South, and W for West).

  • department: the name of the department.

  • crime_person: population per crime against persons (for example, a crime per person value of 20000 indicates that there was one crime against a person for every 20000 people in the department.

  • crime_property: population per crime against property.

  • literacy: the percentage of military conscripts who can read and write.

  • donations: the number of donations to the poor.

  • illegit_birth: population per illegitimate birth.

  • suicides: population per suicide.

  • size_city: the size of the largest city within the department. This variable is a factor with three levels: 1 for the 10 smallest sizes, 2 for the middle 65 department sizes, and 3 for the 10 largest sizes.

  • sex_workers: the number of sex workers registered in Paris from 1816 to 1834, according to the department of each sex worker's birth.

  • distance_to_paris: the distance of the department centroid to Paris, in kilometers.

  • area: the area of the department, in thousands of kilometers squared.

  • population_1831: the population of the department in the year 1831.

  • geometry: information giving the polygonal shape of the county or city district.

Source

Data were modified from the geodaData R package. The original source of the data is the Guerry R package by Michael Friendly and Stephane Dray.

References

Guerry, A.-M. (1833). Essai sur la statistique morale de la France Paris: Crochard. English translation: Hugh P. Whitt and Victor W. Reinking, Lewiston, N.Y. : Edwin Mellen Press, 2002.
